label: thm:fractional-stam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fractional-stam}
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be Boolean independent self-adjoint random variables with symmetric laws and let $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}.$ For any $A\subseteq[n]$, set $S_A=\sum_{i\in A}X_i.$ Let $\mathcal C$ be a collection of nonempty subsets of $[n]$, and let $(\beta_A)_{A\in\mathcal C}$ be a fractional partition, namely
$$
\beta_A\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{A\in\mathcal C:\,i\in A}\beta_A=1
\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n.
$$
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fractional stam}
    \frac{1}{\Psi(S_{[n]})}\geq\sum_{A\in\mathcal C}\frac{\beta_A}{\Psi(S_A)}.
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: thm:entropy-convergence
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:entropy-convergence}
Let $\mu$ and $\mu_t$ be as defined above. If $\Gamma(\mu)>-\infty$, then
\[
 \Gamma(\mu_t)\longrightarrow\Gamma(\mathbf{b})=0.
\]
If $\Gamma(\mu)=-\infty$, then $\Gamma(\mu_t)=-\infty$ for every $t\ge1$.

label: lem:stieltjes
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $x,y>0$, the elementary identity
\[
 \frac{\log x-\log y}{x-y}
 =\int_0^\infty\frac{ds}{(x+s)(y+s)}
\]
allows us, by Fubini's theorem, to obtain the first equality in \eqref{eq:stieltjes} and hence the representation in terms of $r_\rho$. Since $h_\rho(s)\le s^{-1}$, we have $r_\rho(s)\ge0$. Finally, differentiation gives
\[
 r_\rho'(s)
 =\frac{\displaystyle\int (x+s)^{-2}\,d\rho(x)}{\displaystyle\left(\int (x+s)^{-1}\,d\rho(x)\right)^2}-1\ge0
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz.
head: environment

label: lem:boolean-power
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $K_{\rho^{\uplus c}}=cK_\rho$, we have $r_{\rho^{\uplus c}}(s)=cr_\rho(s)$. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{lem:stieltjes} and the change of variables $s=ca$,
\[
 \Psi^{(2)}(\rho^{\uplus c})
 =\int_0^\infty\frac{ds}{(s+cr_\rho(s))^2}
 =\frac1c\int_0^\infty\frac{da}{(a+r_\rho(ca))^2}.
\]
The monotonicity of $r_\rho$ gives $r_\rho(ca)\ge r_\rho(a)$, proving the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:representation relative entropy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that if $m_2(\mu)=1$, one has
$$
\Gamma(\mu\mid\mathbf b) =-\Gamma(\mu),
\qquad
\Gamma(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R}\log|x|\,d\mu(x),
$$
For every $x\neq0$, note that the following identity holds
$$
\log|x|
=
\frac12\int_0^\infty
\left(\frac{1}{1+s}-\frac{1}{x^2+s}\right)\,ds,
$$
which follows from
$$
\int_0^\infty
\left(\frac{1}{s+a}-\frac{1}{s+b}\right)\,ds
=\log\frac{b}{a},
\qquad a,b>0.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\Gamma(\mu)
=
\frac12\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\int_0^\infty
\left(\frac{1}{1+s}-\frac{1}{x^2+s}\right)
\,ds\,d\mu(x).
$$
Since $\Gamma(\mu)>-\infty$, the interchange of the two
integrals is justified by splitting the integral into the regions
$|x|\leq1$ and $|x|>1$. Indeed,
$$
\int_0^\infty
\left|
\frac{1}{1+s}-\frac{1}{x^2+s}
\right|\,ds
=2|\log|x||,
$$
and $\log^+|x|$ is integrable whenever $\mu$ has finite second
moment, while $\Gamma(\mu)>-\infty$ guarantees the integrability
of $\log^-|x|$.
Hence
$$
\Gamma(\mu)
=
\frac12\int_0^\infty
\left(
\frac{1}{1+s}
-
\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x^2+s}\,d\mu(x)
\right)\,ds,
$$
which yields the desired formula.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The representation in Lemma \ref{lem:representation relative entropy} admits a useful interpretation in terms of the nonmicrostates Boolean Fisher information. Recall that for a probability measure $\mu$, the nonmicrostates Fisher information of $\mu$ is defined as
    $$
    \Psi^*(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{1}{x^2}\,d\mu(x).
    $$
    Now let $(\tilde{\mu}_t)_{t\geq0}$ be the flow defined by
    $$
    \tilde{\mu}_t=(T_t)_\#\mu,
    \quad T_t(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)\sqrt{x^2+t}.
    $$
    That is, $\tilde{\mu}_t^{(2)}=(x\mapsto x+t)_\#\mu^{(2)},$ and hence
    $$
    \Psi^*(\tilde{\mu}_t)=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x^2}\,d\tilde{\mu}_t(x)=\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{x+t}\,d\mu^{(2)}(x)=h_{\mu^{(2)}}(t).
    $$
    Moreover,
    $$
    \frac{d}{dt}\Gamma(\tilde{\mu}_t)=\frac12\Psi^*(\tilde{\mu}_t).
    $$
    Indeed, $T_t'(x)=1/(2T_t(x))$, and therefore
    $$
    \frac{d}{dt}\log|T_t(x)|=\frac{1}{2T_t(x)^2}.
    $$
    This should be compared with the nonmicrostates de Bruijn identity along the Boolean heat flow established in~\cite{CebronPan2026}.
head: environment

label: eq:r-additive
title: Proof
body_md:
First assume that $\Psi(X_i)<\infty$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n.$ By the Stam inequality \eqref{eq:stam ineq}, we have $\Psi(S_A)<\infty$ for all $A\subset [n]$. Set $\rho_i=\mathcal L(X_i^2),$ $\rho_A=\mathcal L(S_A^2)$. By \eqref{eq:square-convolution},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:r-additive}
    K_{\rho_A}=\sum_{i\in A}K_{\rho_i},
 \qquad
 r_{\rho_A}(s)=\sum_{i\in A}r_{\rho_i}(s).
\end{equation}
Thus Lemma \ref{lem:stieltjes} gives
\[
 \Psi(S_A)=\int_0^\infty
 \frac{ds}{\left(s+\sum_{i\in A}r_{\rho_i}(s)\right)^2}.
\]
Since each $r_{\rho_i}$ is nonnegative,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:monotone-psi}
    A\subseteq B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Psi(S_B)\le\Psi(S_A).
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 a_A=\frac1{\Psi(S_A)}>0,
 \qquad
 T=\sum_{A\in\mathcal C}\beta_Aa_A.
\]
If $a_A\ge T$ for some $A$, then \eqref{eq:monotone-psi} immediately gives
\[
 \frac1{\Psi(S_{[n]})}\ge a_A\ge T.
\]
We may therefore assume $a_A<T$ for every $A$. Define
\[
 c_A=\frac{T}{a_A}>1,
 \qquad
 w_A=\frac{\beta_Aa_A}{T}.
\]
Then $\sum_Aw_A=1$ and $w_Ac_A=\beta_A$.
Let $\tilde\rho_A=\rho_A^{\uplus c_A}$. By the definition of fractional partition and \eqref{eq:r-additive},
\[
 \sum_Aw_AK_{\tilde\rho_A}
 =\sum_A\beta_AK_{\rho_A}
 =\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{A\ni i}\beta_A\right)K_{\rho_i}
 =K_{\rho_{[n]}}.
\]
Since $K_\rho(z)=z-F_\rho(z)$ and $\sum_A w_A=1$, we obtain
\[
F_{\rho_{[n]}}(z)=\sum_A w_A F_{\tilde\rho_A}(z).
\]
Evaluating at $z=-s$ for $s>0$, we have
$F_{\rho_{[n]}}(-s)<0$ and $F_{\tilde\rho_A}(-s)<0$ for every $A$. Since $x\mapsto x^{-2}$ is convex on $(-\infty,0)$, Jensen's inequality therefore gives
\[
 G_{\rho_{[n]}}(-s)^2
 \le\sum_Aw_AG_{\tilde\rho_A}(-s)^2.
\]
Integrating with respect to $s$ and applying Lemma \ref{lem:stieltjes} and Lemma \ref{lem:boolean-power},
\[
 \Psi(S_{[n]})
 \le\sum_Aw_A\Psi^{(2)}(\tilde\rho_A)
 \le\sum_A\frac{w_A}{c_A}\Psi^{(2)}(\rho_A)
 =\frac1T.
\]
Taking reciprocals yields the desired inequality.

If \(\Psi(X_i)=\infty\) for some \(i\in[n]\), we regularize the corresponding law by setting \(\rho_i(\varepsilon):=\rho_i\uplus\delta_\varepsilon\). Then \(r_{\rho_i(\varepsilon)}(s)=r_{\rho_i}(s+\varepsilon)\). Applying the previous argument to the perturbed laws and then by Lemma \ref{lem:stieltjes}, letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the monotone convergence theorem completes the proof.

label: cor:leave-one-out
title: Corollary
head: environment

label: cor:weighted-stam
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:weighted-stam}
Under the assumptions of Corollary \ref{cor:leave-one-out}, let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{n})\in\mathbb R^{n}$ satisfy $\sum_i a_i^2=1$, and set $S_a=\sum_i a_iX_i$. For $|a_j|<1$, define
\[
 S_a^{(j)}=\frac1{\sqrt{1-a_j^2}}\sum_{i\ne j}a_iX_i.
\]
Then
\[
 \frac1{\Psi(S_a)}
 \ge\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1-a_j^2}{\Psi(S_a^{(j)})},
\]
where terms with $a_j^2=1$ are omitted, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted stam}
    \Psi(S_a)\le\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1-a_j^2)\Psi(S_a^{(j)}).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Corollary \ref{cor:leave-one-out} to $a_1X_1,\ldots,a_{n}X_{n}$. By scaling,
\[
 \frac1{\Psi\left(\sum_{i\ne j}a_iX_i\right)}
 =\frac{1-a_j^2}{\Psi(S_a^{(j)})},
\]
which gives the reciprocal inequality. Setting $p_j=(1-a_j^2)/(n-1)$, we have $p_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$. The weighted harmonic-arithmetic mean inequality then yields the second bound.
head: environment

label: cor:weighted-entropy
title: Corollary
head: environment

label: eq:weighted-fisher-debruijn
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B_1,\ldots,B_{n}$ be Boolean independent Rademacher variables independent of the $X_i$. The square-convolution identity shows that both
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^{n}a_iB_i
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \frac1{\sqrt{1-a_j^2}}\sum_{i\ne j}a_iB_i
\]
have the Rademacher law. Applying the weighted Stam inequality \eqref{eq:weighted stam} to $X_i+\sqrt s B_i$ gives, for $s>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-fisher-debruijn}
    \Psi(S_a+\sqrt s B)
 \le\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1-a_j^2)
 \Psi(S_a^{(j)}+\sqrt s B_j').
\end{equation}
Subtracting from $(1+s)^{-1}$, integrating in $s$, and using the Boolean de Bruijn identity \eqref{eq:debruijn} yields the stated entropy inequality.
head: environment

label: cor:epine-many
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
 N_j=e^{2\Gamma(S_n^{(j)})},
 \qquad
 N=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}N_j.
\]
If $N_j\ge N$ for some $j$, then \eqref{eq:boolean entropy power} gives $e^{2\Gamma(S_n)}\ge N$. Otherwise define $q_j=N_j/N$ and $a_j=\sqrt{1-q_j}$. Since $\sum_jq_j=n-1$, we have $\sum_ja_j^2=1$. Applying Corollary \ref{cor:weighted-entropy} to the rescaled variables $a_j^{-1}X_j$ gives
\[
 \Gamma(S_n)
 \ge\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_j
 \Gamma\bigl(q_j^{-1/2}S_n^{(j)}\bigr).
\]
Using scaling once more,
\[
 \Gamma(S_n)
 \ge\frac1{n-1}\sum_jq_j
 \left(\Gamma(S_n^{(j)})-\frac12\log q_j\right)
 =\frac12\log N.
\]
Exponentiating proves the result.
head: environment

label: eq:ht-derivative
title: Proof
body_md:
For any $s>0$, set
\[
 h_t(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{d\mu_t(x)}{x^2+s}=-\mathrm{Im} \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}}G_{\mu_t}(i\sqrt{s}).
\]
Fix $s>0$. Differentiating with respect to $t$ and using the semigroup relation \eqref{eq:semigroup} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ht-derivative}
    t\partial_th_t(s)
 =-\bigl(\mathrm{Re}\,G_{\mu_t}(i\sqrt s)\bigr)^2
 -s\left(\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{d\mu_t(x)}{(x^2+s)^2}-h_t(s)^2\right).
\end{equation}
The second term on the right-hand side is nonnegative, and we deduce that $t\partial_th_t(s)\le 0$. Moreover,
$$
\operatorname{Re}G_{\mu_t}(i\sqrt s)
=
-\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x}{x^2+s}\,d\mu_t(x).
$$
Therefore, by Cauchy-Schwarz,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\bigl(\operatorname{Re}G_{\mu_t}(i\sqrt s)\bigr)^2
&\leq
\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x^2}{(x^2+s)^2}\,d\mu_t(x)\\
&=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\left(
\frac{1}{x^2+s}
-\frac{s}{(x^2+s)^2}
\right)d\mu_t(x)\\
&=
h_t(s)-s\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{d\mu_t(x)}{(x^2+s)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substituting this inequality into \eqref{eq:ht-derivative} yields
$$
-h_t(s)\le t\partial_t h_t(s)\le0.
$$
The right-hand inequality implies that $t\mapsto h_t(s)$ is decreasing. For the left-hand inequality, we observe that
$
\partial_t\bigl(t h_t(s)\bigr)
=h_t(s)+t\partial_t h_t(s)\ge0.
$
Thus $t\mapsto t h_t(s)$ is increasing, which implies that
$t h_t(s)\ge h_1(s),$ and consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ht-bounds}
    \frac1t h_1(s)\le h_t(s)\le h_1(s),\quad t\ge1.
\end{equation}

For $\varepsilon>0$, introduce the regularized logarithmic integral
\[
\Gamma_\varepsilon(\nu)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\log(x^2+\varepsilon)\,d\nu(x).
\]
Tonelli's theorem gives,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:regularized-entropy}
    \Gamma_\varepsilon(\mu_t)-\Gamma(\mu_t)
 =\frac12\int_0^\varepsilon h_t(s)\,ds.
\end{equation}

Assume first that $\Gamma(\mu)>-\infty$. Taking $t=1$ in \eqref{eq:regularized-entropy} shows that $h_1$ is integrable on every interval $(0,\varepsilon)$. For fixed $s>0$, weak convergence $\mu_t\Rightarrow \mathbf{b}$ gives
\[
 h_t(s)\longrightarrow h_\infty(s)=\frac1{1+s}.
\]
The upper bound in \eqref{eq:ht-bounds} and dominated convergence therefore yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:regularized-limit}
    \Gamma_\varepsilon(\mu_t)-\Gamma(\mu_t)
 \longrightarrow
 \frac12\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{ds}{1+s}
 =\frac12\log(1+\varepsilon).
\end{equation}
On the other hand, for sufficiently large $M>0$, decompose 
$$
\Gamma_\varepsilon(\mu_t)=\frac{1}{2}\int \log (x^2+\varepsilon)\wedge M\,d\mu_t(x)+\frac{1}{2}\int (\log (x^2+\varepsilon)-\log (x^2+\varepsilon)\wedge M)\,d\mu_t(x).
$$
Since the family $\{\mu_t\}_{t\ge1}$ has uniformly bounded second moments, it is uniformly integrable. Thus, the second term can be made uniformly arbitrarily small. The first term tends to $\Gamma_\varepsilon(\mathbf{b})$ by the weak convergence $\mu_t\Rightarrow \mathbf{b}$. Therefore, letting $M\to \infty$ yields
\[
\Gamma_\varepsilon(\mu_t)\longrightarrow\Gamma_\varepsilon(\mathbf{b})=\frac12\log(1+\varepsilon).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:regularized-limit} proves $\Gamma(\mu_t)\longrightarrow0$.

Now assume $\Gamma(\mu)=-\infty$. Then \eqref{eq:regularized-entropy} at $t=1$ implies
\[
 \int_0^\varepsilon h_1(s)\,ds=\infty.
\]
The lower bound in \eqref{eq:ht-bounds} gives
\[
 \int_0^\varepsilon h_t(s)\,ds
 \ge \frac1t\int_0^\varepsilon h_1(s)\,ds
 =\infty.
\]
Since $\Gamma_\varepsilon(\mu_t)$ is finite, \eqref{eq:regularized-entropy} forces $\Gamma(\mu_t)=-\infty$.
head: environment

label: eq:f_n
title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:Nevanlinna repre P_0,1}, let $\nu$ be such that $F_\mu(z)=z-G_\nu(z),$ and hence
\begin{equation*}
G_n(z):=G_{\mu_n}(z)
=\frac{1}{z-\sqrt n\,G_\nu(\sqrt n z)}.
\end{equation*}
Write $b_3=m_1(\nu)=m_3(\mu),\ b_4=
m_2(\nu)=m_4(\mu)-1$. For any $s>0$, define
\[
R_s:=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x}{x^2+s^2}\,d\nu(x),
\qquad
I_s:=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{x^2+s^2}\,d\nu(x),
\]
so that $G_\nu(is)=-R_s-isI_s.$ By Lemma \ref{lem:representation relative entropy}, after the change of variables
$s\mapsto s^2/n$, \eqref{eq:relative-entropy-integral} becomes
\begin{equation*}
\Gamma(\mu_n\mid\mathbf b)
=
\int_0^\infty
\frac{s}{n}
\left(
f_n(s)-\frac{n}{n+s^2}
\right)\,ds,
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f_n}
f_n(s)
:=h_n\left(\frac{s^2}{n}\right)=-\operatorname{Im}\frac{1}{s/\sqrt n}
G_n\left(\frac{is}{\sqrt n}\right)=
\frac{I_s+n^{-1}}
{R_s^2+s^2(I_s+n^{-1})^2}.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{The compact region.}
Fix $M>0$. By Jensen's inequality,
\[
I_s
\geq \frac{1}{b_4+s^2}
\geq \frac{1}{b_4+M^2},
\qquad 0<s\leq M.
\]
Hence, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$I_s\geq n^{-1}$ on $(0,M]$, and therefore
\[
f_n(s)\leq 2f_\infty(s),
\qquad
f_\infty(s):=
\frac{I_s}{R_s^2+s^2I_s^2}.
\]
On the other hand, $F_\mu(is)
=
is-G_\nu(is)
=
R_s+is(1+I_s),$ so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ImGmu}
-\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(is)
=
\frac{s(1+I_s)}
{R_s^2+s^2(1+I_s)^2}.
\end{equation}
By the lower bound $I_s\geq (b_4+M^2)^{-1}$, there exists a constant $C_M>1$ such that $1+I_s\leq C_M I_s$ for all $0<s\leq M,$ and consequently $sf_\infty(s)\leq C^2_M\bigl[-\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(is)\bigr].$
Moreover, note that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^M-\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(is)\,ds
&=
\int_{\mathbb R}
\left(
\int_0^M\frac{s}{x^2+s^2}\,ds
\right)d\mu(x)\\
&=
\frac12
\int_{\mathbb R}
\log\left(1+\frac{M^2}{x^2}\right)d\mu(x)
<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the finiteness follows from $\Gamma(\mu)>-\infty$.
Thus
\[
\int_0^M \frac{s}{n} f_n(s)\,ds=O_M(n^{-1}).
\]
Finally, 
\[
\int_0^M
\frac{s}{n}\frac{n}{n+s^2}\,ds
=
\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{M^2}{n}\right)
=
O_M(n^{-1}).
\] 
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact}
\int_0^M
\frac{s}{n}
\left|
f_n(s)-\frac{n}{n+s^2}
\right|\,ds
=
O_M(n^{-1}),
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Expansion on the tail.}
We now consider $s\geq M$, and set $A_n(s):=s^{-2}+n^{-1}.$ Since $m_2(\nu)=b_4$,
\[
I_s=s^{-2}-b_4s^{-4}+\varepsilon_s,
\qquad
\varepsilon_s:=
s^{-4}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x^4}{x^2+s^2}\,d\nu(x).
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eps-bound}
0\leq\varepsilon_s\leq b_4s^{-4},
\qquad
s^4\varepsilon_s
=
\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x^4}{x^2+s^2}\,d\nu(x)
\xrightarrow[s\to\infty]{}0,
\end{equation}
where the convergence follows from the dominated convergence theorem.

Similarly,
\[
R_s=b_3s^{-2}+\eta_s,
\qquad
\eta_s:=
-s^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x^3}{x^2+s^2}\,d\nu(x).
\]
By $|x|/(x^2+s^2)\leq 1/(2s)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eta-bound}
|\eta_s|
\leq
\frac{b_4}{2}s^{-3}.
\end{equation}

Set
\[
d_s:=I_s-s^{-2}=-b_4s^{-4}+\varepsilon_s.
\]
Then $I_s+n^{-1}=A_n(s)+d_s$, and \eqref{eq:f_n} gives
\[
f_n(s)
=
\frac{s^{-2}(A_n(s)+d_s)}
{s^{-2}R_s^2+(A_n(s)+d_s)^2}.
\]
Let
\[
B_n(s):=s^{-2}R_s^2+(A_n(s)+d_s)^2.
\]
Since $\frac{n}{n+s^2}=\frac{s^{-2}}{A_n(s)},$ we have the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-difference}
f_n(s)-\frac{s^{-2}}{A_n(s)}
=-\frac{s^{-2}\bigl(A_n(s)d_s+d_s^2+s^{-2}R_s^2\bigr)}
{A_n(s)B_n(s)}.
\end{equation}

Write
\[
R_s^2=b_3^2s^{-4}+\delta_s,
\qquad
\delta_s:=R_s^2-b_3^2s^{-4}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:eta-bound},
\[
|\delta_s|
\leq
2|b_3|s^{-2}|\eta_s|+\eta_s^2
\leq C_\mu s^{-5}.
\]
Substituting
\[
d_s=-b_4s^{-4}+\varepsilon_s,
\qquad
R_s^2=b_3^2s^{-4}+\delta_s
\]
into \eqref{eq:exact-difference}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_n(s)-\frac{s^{-2}}{A_n(s)}
={}&
\frac{b_4s^{-6}}{B_n(s)}
-\frac{b_3^2s^{-8}}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}
-\frac{s^{-2}\varepsilon_s}{B_n(s)}\\
&-\frac{s^{-2}d_s^2}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}
-\frac{s^{-4}\delta_s}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, if we define
\begin{align*}
\xi_n(s):={}&
b_4s^{-6}
\left(\frac{1}{B_n(s)}-\frac{1}{A_n(s)^2}\right)\\
&+b_3^2s^{-8}
\left(\frac{1}{A_n(s)^3}
-\frac{1}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}\right)
-\frac{s^{-2}\varepsilon_s}{B_n(s)}\\
&-\frac{s^{-2}d_s^2}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}
-\frac{s^{-4}\delta_s}{A_n(s)B_n(s)},
\end{align*}
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:asymptotic-decomp}
f_n(s)-\frac{s^{-2}}{A_n(s)}
=
\frac{b_4s^{-6}}{A_n(s)^2}
-\frac{b_3^2s^{-8}}{A_n(s)^3}
+\xi_n(s).
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Estimate of the remainder.}
From \eqref{eq:eps-bound} and \eqref{eq:eta-bound}, there exists some constant $C_\mu>0$ such that
\[
|d_s|\leq C_\mu s^{-4},
\qquad
|R_s|\leq C_\mu s^{-2}.
\]
Since $A_n(s)\geq s^{-2}$, for $M$ sufficiently large,
\[
|d_s|\leq \frac{A_n(s)}{2},
\qquad
s^{-2}R_s^2\leq \frac{A_n(s)^2}{4}.
\]
Hence
\[
cA_n(s)^2\leq B_n(s)\leq CA_n(s)^2
\]
for some constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $\mu$. Moreover,
\[
B_n(s)-A_n(s)^2
=
2A_n(s)d_s+d_s^2+s^{-2}R_s^2,
\]
so that
\[
|B_n(s)-A_n(s)^2|
\leq C_\mu A_n(s)s^{-4}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\left|
\frac{1}{B_n(s)}-\frac{1}{A_n(s)^2}
\right|
\leq
C_\mu\frac{s^{-4}}{A_n(s)^3},
\qquad
\left|
\frac{1}{A_n(s)^3}
-\frac{1}{A_n(s)B_n(s)}
\right|
\leq
C_\mu\frac{s^{-4}}{A_n(s)^4}.
\]

For fixed $M$, let
\[
\theta_M:=
\sup_{s\geq M}s^4\varepsilon_s.
\]
By \eqref{eq:eps-bound}, $\theta_M\to0$ as $M\to\infty$. Using the previous estimates and $|d_s|\leq C_\mu s^{-4}$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\xi_n(s)|
\leq C_\mu\Bigg(
\frac{s^{-10}}{A_n(s)^3}
+\frac{s^{-12}}{A_n(s)^4}
+\theta_M\frac{s^{-6}}{A_n(s)^2}+\frac{s^{-10}}{A_n(s)^3}
+\frac{s^{-9}}{A_n(s)^3}
\Bigg).
\end{aligned}
\]
With the change of variable $u=s^{-2}$, we have
\[
\frac{s}{n}\,ds=-\frac{1}{2n}u^{-2}\,du,
\]
and it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_M^\infty\frac{s}{n}|\xi_n(s)|\,ds
\leq \frac{C_\mu}{n}\Bigg[
&\int_0^{M^{-2}}\frac{u^3}{(u+n^{-1})^3}\,du+\int_0^{M^{-2}}\frac{u^4}{(u+n^{-1})^4}\,du
+\theta_M\int_0^{M^{-2}}
\frac{u}{(u+n^{-1})^2}\,du\\ &+\int_0^{M^{-2}}\frac{u^3}{(u+n^{-1})^3}\,du+\int_0^{M^{-2}}\frac{u^{5/2}}{(u+n^{-1})^3}\,du
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\]
The first, second, fourth and fifth integrals are uniformly bounded in $n$, while
\[
\int_0^{M^{-2}}
\frac{u}{(u+n^{-1})^2}\,du
=
\log n+O_M(1).
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:remainder-o}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{n}{\log n}
\int_M^\infty\frac{s}{n}|\xi_n(s)|\,ds
\leq C_\mu\theta_M.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Integration of the leading terms.}
From \eqref{eq:asymptotic-decomp}, the two leading contributions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{4,n}(M)
&:=
\int_M^\infty
\frac{s}{n}\frac{b_4s^{-6}}{A_n(s)^2}\,ds\\
&=
\frac{nb_4}{2}
\int_{M^2}^\infty\frac{dy}{y(n+y)^2},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{3,n}(M)
&:=
-\int_M^\infty
\frac{s}{n}\frac{b_3^2s^{-8}}{A_n(s)^3}\,ds\\
&=
-\frac{n^2b_3^2}{2}
\int_{M^2}^\infty\frac{dy}{y(n+y)^3},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $y=s^2$. Using the elementary decompositions
\[
\frac{1}{y(n+y)^2}
=
\frac{1}{n^2}\frac{1}{y}
-\frac{1}{n^2}\frac{1}{n+y}
-\frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{(n+y)^2},
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{y(n+y)^3}
=&
\frac{1}{n^3}\frac{1}{y}
-\frac{1}{n^3}\frac{1}{n+y}-\frac{1}{n^2}\frac{1}{(n+y)^2}
-\frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{(n+y)^3},
\end{aligned}
\]
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T4}
T_{4,n}(M)
=
\frac{b_4}{2}\frac{\log n}{n}
+O_M(n^{-1}),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T3}
T_{3,n}(M)
=
-\frac{b_3^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n}
+O_M(n^{-1}).
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{eq:compact}, \eqref{eq:remainder-o}, \eqref{eq:T4}, and \eqref{eq:T3}, we deduce that
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{n}{\log n}\Gamma(\mu_n\mid\mathbf b)-\frac{b_4-b_3^2}{2}\right|
\leq C_\mu\theta_M.
\]
Finally, letting $M\to\infty$ and using $\theta_M\to0$, we conclude that
\[
\Gamma(\mu_n\mid\mathbf b) = \frac{b_4-b_3^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n} +o\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right),
\]
as claimed.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:four-point}
Fix $d\in(0,1)$ and consider
\[
 \nu_d=\frac14\bigl(\delta_{\sqrt{1+d}}+\delta_{-\sqrt{1+d}}+\delta_{\sqrt{1-d}}+\delta_{-\sqrt{1-d}}\bigr).
\]
Write $\nu_{d,n}=D_{n^{-1/2}}(\nu_d^{\uplus n})$. Then
\[
 \Gamma(\nu_{d,n})=-\frac{d^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n}+O\!\left(\frac1n\right),
\]
head: environment
name: Sharpness of the entropic rate

title: Proof
body_md:
A direct calculation gives
\[
 G_{\nu_d}(w)=\frac{w(w^2-1)}{(w^2-1)^2-d^2},
 \qquad
 F_{\nu_d}(w)=w-\frac1w-\frac{d^2}{w(w^2-1)}.
\]
Using the Boolean convolution and dilation identities,
\[
 F_{\nu_{d,n}}(z)
 =z-\frac1z-\frac{d^2}{z(nz^2-1)},
 \]
and therefore
\[
 G_{\nu_{d,n}}(z)
 =\frac{z(nz^2-1)}{(z^2-1)(nz^2-1)-d^2}.
\]
Set
\[
 \Delta_n=\sqrt{(n-1)^2+4nd^2},
 \qquad
 u_{\pm,n}=\frac{n+1\pm\Delta_n}{2n},
\]
and
\[
 \omega_{+,n}=\frac{n-1+\Delta_n}{2\Delta_n},
 \qquad
 \omega_{-,n}=\frac{\Delta_n-(n-1)}{2\Delta_n}.
\]
Partial fractions give
\[
 \nu_{d,n}
 =\frac{\omega_{+,n}}{2}(\delta_{\sqrt{u_{+,n}}}+\delta_{-\sqrt{u_{+,n}}})
 +\frac{\omega_{-,n}}{2}(\delta_{\sqrt{u_{-,n}}}+\delta_{-\sqrt{u_{-,n}}}).
\]
Hence
\[
 \Gamma(\nu_{d,n})
 =\frac{\omega_{+,n}}{2}\log u_{+,n}+\frac{\omega_{-,n}}{2}\log u_{-,n}.
\]
As $n\to\infty$,
\[
 \Delta_n=n-1+2d^2+O(n^{-1}),
\]
\[
 u_{+,n}=1+\frac{d^2}{n}+O(n^{-2}),
 \qquad
 u_{-,n}=\frac{1-d^2}{n}+O(n^{-2}),
\]
and
\[
 \omega_{+,n}=1-\frac{d^2}{n}+O(n^{-2}),
 \qquad
 \omega_{-,n}=\frac{d^2}{n}+O(n^{-2}).
\]
Substitution yields
\[
 \Gamma(\nu_{d,n})=-\frac{d^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n}+O(n^{-1}).
\]
Since $\nu_{d,n}\in\mathcal{P}_{0,1}(\mathbb{R})$, the identity \eqref{eq:relative entropy} gives
\[
 \Gamma(\nu_{d,n}\mid \mathbf{b})
 =\frac{d^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n}+O(n^{-1}),
\]
as claimed.

label: eq:psi-integral
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\rho=\mu^{(2)}$. Then $\rho$ is supported on $\mathbb{R}_+$, $\int x\,d\rho(x)=1$, and
\[
 \int(x-1)^2\,d\rho(x)=m_4(\mu)-1.
\]
For any $s>0$, set
\[
 h(s)=\int_0^\infty\frac{d\rho(x)}{s+x},
 \qquad
 r(s)=\frac1{h(s)}-s,
 \qquad
 q(s)=1-r(s).
\]
Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \frac1{s+1}\le h(s)<\frac1s,
\]
so $0<r(s)\le1$ and $0\le q(s)<1$. By \eqref{eq:square-convolution},
\[
 \mu_n^{(2)}=D_{1/n}(\rho^{\uplus n}),
 \qquad
 K_{\mu_n^{(2)}}(z)=K_\rho(nz).
\]
Hence, for any $s>0$,
\[
 -G_{\mu_n^{(2)}}(-s)=\frac1{s+r(ns)}.
\]
Applying the change of variables $u = ns$ to the identity $\int_0^\infty (s+1)^{-2} \, ds = 1$, and setting $b_n(u) \coloneqq 1 + u/n$, we have
\begin{equation*}
    1 = \frac{1}{n} \int_0^\infty \frac{du}{b_n(u)^2}.
\end{equation*}
Substituting the identity in the integral representation of $\Psi(\mu_n)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:stieltjes} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:psi-integral}
    \Psi(\mu_n) - 1 = \frac{1}{n} \int_0^\infty H_n(u) \, du,
\end{equation}
where $H_n(u) \coloneqq (b_n(u) - q(u))^{-2} - b_n(u)^{-2}$. A straightforward calculation gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:Hn}
    H_n(u) &= \frac{b_n(u)^2 - (b_n(u) - q(u))^2}{b_n(u)^2 (b_n(u) - q(u))^2} \nonumber \\
    &= q(u) \frac{2b_n(u) - q(u)}{b_n(u)^2 (b_n(u) - q(u))^2},
\end{align}
Recall that $b_4=m_4(\mu)-1.$ We first establish the following asymptotic behavior of $q$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-asymptotic}
    \lim_{u\to \infty}uq(u)=b_4.
\end{equation}
Indeed, a rearrangement gives
\[
 q(u)=\frac{(u+1)h(u)-1}{h(u)},
\]
and by $\int(x-1)d\rho(x)=0$, we have
\[
 uq(u)
 =\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{u(x-1)^2}{u+x}\,d\rho(x)}{\displaystyle(u+1)\int_0^\infty\frac1{u+x}\,d\rho(x)}.
\]
The dominated convergence theorem yields \eqref{eq:q-asymptotic}. If $b_4=0$, then $\rho=\delta_1$ and symmetry forces $\mu=\mathbf{b}$, so the conclusion is immediate. Assume henceforth $b_4>0$, and it remains to prove
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hn-asymptotic}
    \frac{1}{n}\int_0^\infty H_n(u)\,du
 =2b_4\frac{\log n}{n}+o\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right).
\end{equation}

We split the integral into a bounded part, an intermediate bulk, and a tail.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Bounded region.}
From \eqref{eq:Hn}, $0\le H_n(u)\le r(u)^{-2}.$ Moreover, $r(s)/s=(sh(s))^{-1}-1$ is decreasing in $s$, since $sh(s)$ is increasing in $s$. Thus for any $0<u\le M$,
\[
 r(u)\ge\frac{r(M)}M u,
 \qquad
 u+r(u)\le\left(1+\frac M{r(M)}\right)r(u).
\]
Since
\[
 \Psi(\mu)=\int_0^\infty\frac{du}{(u+r(u))^2}<\infty,
\]
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bounded-Hn}
    \sup_{n\ge1}\int_0^M H_n(u)\,du<\infty.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Bulk region.}
Fix $\eta\in(0,b_4)$. By \eqref{eq:q-asymptotic}, there exists some sufficiently large $M$ such that
\[
 \frac{b_4-\eta}{u}\le q(u)\le\frac{b_4+\eta}{u}
\qquad (u\ge M).
\]
For $M\le u\le\delta n$, write
\[
 H_n(u)=q(u)\Phi(b_n(u),q(u)),
 \qquad
 \Phi(b,q)=\frac{2b-q}{b^2(b-q)^2}.
\]
Because $\Phi(1,0)=2$, one may first choose $M$ large and then $\delta>0$ small enough that
\[
 2-\eta\le \Phi(b_n(u),q(u))\le2+\eta
\]
uniformly on $[M,\delta n]$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bulk-Hn}
    (2-\eta)(b_4-\eta)
 \log\frac{\delta n}{M}
 \le\int_M^{\delta n}H_n(u)\,du
 \le(2+\eta)(b_4+\eta)
 \log\frac{\delta n}{M}.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Tail.}
Again by \eqref{eq:q-asymptotic}, there exists $C>0$ such that $q(u)\le C/u$ for $u\ge M$. For fixed $\delta>0$ and sufficiently large $n$, $u\ge\delta n$ implies $q(u)\le1/2$, and hence
\[
 H_n(u)\le\frac{8q(u)}{(1+u/n)^3}
 \le\frac{8C}{u(1+u/n)^3}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tail-Hn}
    \int_{\delta n}^\infty H_n(u)\,du
 \le 8C\int_\delta^\infty\frac{dv}{v(1+v)^3}
 =O_\delta(1).
\end{equation}
Dividing \eqref{eq:bounded-Hn}, \eqref{eq:bulk-Hn}, and \eqref{eq:tail-Hn} by $ n$, then letting $n\to\infty$ and $\eta\downarrow0$, yields \eqref{eq:Hn-asymptotic}. Substitution into \eqref{eq:psi-integral} gives
\[
 \Psi(\mu_n)-1
 =2b_4\frac{\log n}{n}+o\!\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right),
\]
as claimed.
